- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially after spikes.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates or fails to anticipate sharp drops; increase downward bias in early forecast periods.
- Model frequently overreacts to short-term sentiment swings, producing exaggerated overshoots (e.g., 10x+ spikes) that don’t materialize; apply smoothing or decay to sentiment-driven peaks.
- If history shows mean reversion (e.g., prices trending down then stabilizing), model often fails to recognize it; adjust forecasts to align with recent 5–7 day average if sentiment is neutral or mildly positive.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overestimate early periods (e.g., 1–5 days) when sentiment is bullish, then underestimates later periods — apply a “sentiment decay” multiplier to reduce early forecast weights.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral, model often produces erratic forecasts; use sentiment median or weighted average to anchor predictions.
- Avoid forecasting extreme values (e.g., >10x or <0.1x true values) unless sentiment strongly supports it — apply a “clipping” rule to prevent unrealistic extremes.
